tracks.title: The worst-case question
tracks.text: Lesson 02 point 2 — capabilities. A sub-lesson, under the Nexus. The parent lesson made a promise… that for anything running on the engine, the question — what could this thing do, at worst — has a short written answer. This lesson is that answer. [curious] Here is the problem it solves. Every security review of every plugin system arrives at the same question. And most sandboxes answer it with a filter — an allowlist, a permission check, a proxy standing in front of a capability that still exists underneath. Filters have to be audited. Filters have bypasses. The history of sandbox escapes is mostly the history of someone finding the capability behind the check. This ecosystem answers differently. The whole policy is one map literal, in one file, four entries long… and the engine makes those entries true by construction, not by checking.

tracks.title: A profile is three walls
tracks.text: First — a profile is three walls. A capability, here, is a named power the host grants a sandboxed workload at dock time. One word in a profile… turned into the only host imports that exist. An ungranted capability is not denied. It does not exist. A profile bundles three values, and each is a different kind of wall. First, memory — space. Grow past it and the store traps. Second, timeout — time. A wall-clock budget per component call. Third, caps — reach. The words the host links imports from. [curious] And there are exactly four profiles. Minimal… sixty-four megabytes, five seconds, and a working set of caps — the virtual file system, commands, exec, key-value, secrets, queue, and the brokered transports. Network… one hundred twenty-eight megabytes, thirty seconds, and exactly three more words — net, llm, and browse. Posix… two hundred fifty-six megabytes, a full minute, and two more words — posix and parallel. And compute… the restrictive demo rung. Sixty-four megabytes, five seconds, and one single cap — the file system. No exec. No durable storage. No network. Read it as a ladder — each rung adds a few words, some space, and some time. And if you ask for a profile that does not exist… the lookup silently resolves to compute — the vfs-only rung, least privilege, not the broader minimal. Fail closed — and there is a test that pins it. A running engine will even tell you which walls it is behind. Ask an instance for its info and it answers with four things — its id… its profile… its cap list… and a call count. That is the security review, pre-written.

tracks.title: Granted means linked
tracks.text: Now the headline — granted means linked. When a component docks, the host does not install a guard in front of every capability. It builds the imports map — the set of host functions the component can name at all — directly from the cap list. Picture the flow. The base map holds exactly one entry… session info. Always granted, read-only identifiers. Then one reduce walks the cap list, and each word merges in its import. The vfs word brings the query function. Commands brings run-command. Llm brings the completion call. Browse brings fetch. Parallel brings the fan-out. And any word with no component-lane binding falls through… and merges nothing. Then comes the fork. If the component imports a subset of that map — it instantiates, and runs. If it imports even one word more… [excited] it fails to instantiate. Before execution. There is no call to intercept, because the function it asked for was never linked into its world. That is enforcement by construction. Not an if-statement that says no — an absence the workload cannot route around. Two smaller constructions ride along. The session info a component reads holds its id, tenant, and profile — the working directory is deliberately left out, so it can never leak a host path. And standard input and output are simply not inherited. Everything else is not forbidden. It is missing from the membrane.

tracks.title: The wall, not the meter
tracks.text: Next wall — memory. The wall, not the meter. Each profile number becomes a store limit on the wasm store itself, wired the same way in all three dock lanes. A workload that tries to grow past its cap does not get throttled, and does not get swapped. The store traps. And here is what happens next, for everyone else on the engine. The trap surfaces as an error tuple to the caller… and the supervisor decides. Restart, retire, report. The BEAM survives. The neighbors never notice. A memory bomb in one workbook is a return value in one process — not an out-of-memory event on the machine. One honesty note, because this lesson deals in evidence. The trap-on-grow behavior is asserted in the engine module docs and wired in three places… but it does not have a dedicated regression test the way the network gate does. The claim is the design. The strongest proof on this page lives two walls over.

tracks.title: The runaway trap
tracks.text: The second wall — time. The runaway trap. Component calls do not run on a BEAM scheduler. They run on a tokio thread inside wasmtime — which is exactly why an infinite loop in a component cannot wedge the engine. The profile timeout is a wall-clock budget for one component call, passed straight into stock Wasmex. No fork. And the entire mechanism is four lines of code… a timeout argument on the call, and one catch clause that turns the exit into an error tuple — cpu timeout. The engine ships a live demo, and the numbers tell the story. Start an instance named runaway, on minimal, with a budget of eight hundred milliseconds. Tell it to spin. About eight hundred milliseconds later, the caller gets back the error tuple — trapped at the boundary. Then start a second instance, named healthy… and it answers immediately. [chuckles] The runaway got exactly its budget, the caller got an error instead of a hang, and the misbehaving code never got a veto over anyone else. There is a second mechanism in this family — fuel. Deterministic instruction metering. But Wasmex zero point fourteen only surfaces fuel on core-module stores, not component stores. So fuel-capped core modules are how the package manager caps tool modules — the demo sets five million units and an infinite loop traps — while components get the wall clock. Two lanes, two mechanisms… by constraint, not preference.

tracks.title: The one network switch
tracks.text: The third wall has a single switch — the network. Whether a workload gets an ambient network stack at all is one derived boolean. In speech, it reads… allow http is true when the cap list contains net, or browse. Only the network and posix profiles qualify. And the punchline is what that one boolean controls. In the wasm store builder, the single allow-http flag gates three things at once. First — whether the wasi http import is linked at all. Second — whether the store inherits the host socket pool. Third — whether DNS lookups are allowed. False means no http import… no socket pool… no name resolution. A non-network component cannot reach the host network stack at all. The switch does not filter requests. It removes the network from the universe. Now the war story, because this is where the lesson earns your trust. A security pass — finding number seven — caught that instance startup hardcoded allow http to true. [sighs] Every instance, even the most restrictive minimal profile, had full outbound network. The fix is the one derived boolean you just heard… plus a regression suite that pins it from five directions. Minimal refuted. Network and posix asserted. An unknown profile shown to fail closed. A property test that the gate always agrees with the cap list. And a real probe component, instantiated under the tightened minimal profile, proving the fix is not over-broad. That suite is why this lesson gets to say wall without blushing. One precision note. Minimal does carry the words tcp, udp, and tls. In the component lane those bind nothing. In the core-module lanes they bind brokered one-shots — the guest hands the host a destination and bytes… the host resolves the name once, refuses internal addresses, and connects to the pinned IP. Resolve then pin — which defeats DNS rebinding — under rate limits, a one-megabyte cap, a ten-second timeout, and an audit log. Brokered is not ambient. A wall… plus a guarded mail slot.

tracks.title: Three docks, two gating styles
tracks.text: A depth rung now — three docks, two gating styles. One profile table, but three kinds of workload consume it. First, the component lane — wasm components against the engine interface. Gated by presence… imports built from caps, and denial means failing to instantiate before execution. Second, the rust dock — compiled Rust core modules. Also presence — host functions merged per cap word. A clock and a log always… the egress functions only when the http gate passes… and each remaining word merged only when granted. Ask for an ungranted import, and you never start. Third, the javascript dock — QuickJS commands. And this one is the honest exception. The harness always links every host function… but each consults a flag computed once per run from the profile, and a denied capability returns minus one at the boundary — which the shim surfaces as null in the script. [curious] The verdict of that comparison… one policy map, two enforcement styles. Absence at link time where the lane allows it — and a host-side flag where it does not. In every lane, the answer is computed from the same four-entry literal.

tracks.title: What each word buys
tracks.text: Second depth rung — what each word buys. Every cap word is a contract, and the pattern repeats in every row… the sensitive thing stays on the host side of the membrane. A few rows tell the whole story. The vfs word buys SQL against the instance's own SQLite file system — nobody else's. Commands buys trust-aware execution — third-party commands run in a separate VM — and every call logs one step to the telemetry file. Secrets buys signing — HMAC with a named secret the guest can use… but never read. Llm buys completions where the host holds the key — the component never sees it. Net buys ambient http in the core lanes, with an SSRF floor per URL and a hard ceiling of sixty-four URLs per batch call. The transports buy those brokered, pinned, audited one-shots. And parallel buys a fan-out on the BEAM — the parallelism that single-threaded wasm cannot have on its own. [chuckles] Grant the verb… keep the noun. Sign without reading. Complete without the key. Store without naming your own tenant. That is the cap list's whole philosophy in three verbs.

tracks.title: Profiles in the wild
tracks.text: So — profiles in the wild. Who picks one? The host, at dock time. It is an option on instance start… never a property of the file. [chuckles] A workbook cannot grant itself anything. In practice the rungs map to roles. Agents run under the network profile — they need the model call and egress to do their jobs. Builds and resumed sessions start at minimal. And compute is the pure-function rung — a demo, or an untrusted transform that needs a scratch disk and nothing else. For toolkit authors, the cap list is a manifest line — caps, colon, then the words. And the verifier cross-checks it two ways. First… every declared cap must be grantable — known to some profile. Second… at least one profile must grant the whole declared set — otherwise the toolkit can never instantiate anywhere. Picture the verify flow as a fork. Declare vfs, commands, and net… and verification passes, reporting — granted by the network and posix profiles. Declare a set no single profile covers… and it fails, before anything ships. One last distinction, so two dials do not blur into one. Profiles answer — what can it reach. The isolation tiers answer — where does it run. First-party code runs in-instance… third-party in a separate VM. Orthogonal axes. Different lessons.

tracks.title: Honesty
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where the walls are thinner than the prose. [exhales] First… the runaway thread is not freed yet. The wall-clock cap traps the call — the caller gets its error, the BEAM stays responsive — but the worker thread the runaway was spinning on keeps spinning. Epoch interruption, the refinement that frees it, is filed, open work. The trap protects the caller and the engine… not the thread pool. Second… fuel is core-module only. Components get the wall clock. A library constraint, not a choice. Third… four fixed profiles, and no custom ones. You pick a rung. That is a real limitation — and also the point. The worst-case answer stays short because the menu does. Fourth… fail-closed is silent. A typo in a profile name quietly becomes the vfs-only compute rung — least privilege, not the broader minimal. Safe direction — no warning. Fifth… minimal is not zero-network in every lane. The wall removes the ambient stack. Core-module guests still get the brokered, pinned, capped one-shots. No mediated bytes would be a stronger claim — and this lesson does not make it. And sixth… the evidence is uneven. The network gate has a five-way regression suite. The memory trap has module docs and three wiring sites. Both are real. One is proven harder than the other — and you deserve to know which.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can I define my own profile? No. There are four, in a map literal — not a config surface. The worst-case question keeps a short answer precisely because the answer cannot grow. Does minimal really have zero network? In the component lane — yes, literally. No http import, no socket pool, no DNS. In the core lanes — brokered one-shots only, host-resolved and pinned. What happens at the memory cap — an error, or a kill? A trap. The store refuses the growth, the call returns an error tuple, and the supervisor decides. The machine never feels it. Is the timeout per call, or per lifetime? Per component call. Each call gets the budget… the instance lives as long as its supervisor likes. Who picks the profile — the workbook, or the host? The host, at dock time. A toolkit can declare what it needs… but declaration is a request the verifier checks and the installer grants. [chuckles] Never a power.

tracks.title: Back up to the Nexus
tracks.text: So that is capabilities. Three walls — space, time, and reach. Four profiles in one map literal. [curious] And one idea worth keeping… granted means linked. An ungranted capability is not refused — it is absent, and a component that asks for it never runs at all. The way back up is short. This lesson is the mechanism behind one sentence on the Nexus page — capabilities are granted, not inherited. Head back to lesson two for the rest of that picture… the engine, the isolation story, and the residents. And when a toolkit lesson asks you to write a caps line — you now know exactly which profile will answer.
